newsitem.title: FRANCE: Albright to press Bosnia initiative in Paris.
newsitem.headline: Albright to press Bosnia initiative in Paris.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright planned on Monday to press with France and Russia a U.S. initiative to reinvigorate international peace efforts in Bosnia, U.S. officials said.

"We all need to send the same message. We want to put Bosnia back on the front pages of people's attention, " State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said ahead of Albright's Paris meeting with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and a private dinner with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

The NATO-led stabilisation force (SFOR) in Bosnia "is only going to be there another year" and the world needs to act urgently with that June 1998 deadline in mind, he told reporters on Albright's airplane en route from the United States.

Albright arrived in the French capital early on Monday. She plans to attend Tuesday's signing in Paris of the NATO-Russia security agreement setting terms for that key relationship as the Atlantic alliance expands eastward.

But another key theme of her week-long trip to Europe will be the Bosnia initiative that she outlined last week in Washington. The "contact group" of major powers involved in Bosnia -- the United States, France, Britain, Germany and Russia -- are to meet on the subject on Friday in Sintra, Portugal.

As part of the initiative, Albright announced that U.S. troops, the bulk of SFOR, would take on new roles in helping ensure the safe return of war refugees and newly elected local officials and also establish telecommunications links among Bosnia's still-hostile ethnic Moslem, Croat and Serb communities.

In addition, she said, Washington would bring increased financial and other pressures to bear to encourage parties to the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accords -- including Croatia and Serbia as well as the Bosnian factions -- to comply with their commitments.
Many experts see a deepening crisis in Bosnia.

U.S. officials acknowledge that while the Dayton accord ended the Bosnian war, the peace is not secure with signatories resisting integration, return of refugees and cooperation with the international war crimes tribunal at The Hague.

Although experts increasingly see Bosnia being partitioned, Albright said last week that Washington remained committed to a unified state with two entities, one for Serbs and the other a Moslem-Croat federation.

Her talks with de Charette and Primakov are expected to include discussion of a replacement for Carl Bildt as international envoy for Bosnia, who has the difficult but key role of negotiating among Bosnia's factions.
The contact group is expected to make a decision at Friday's meeting. Bildt has delayed his departure for months because contact group members could not agree on a successor.

U.S. officials have not disclosed their choice. But Albright pointedly sidestepped endorsing at a news conference on Friday a man touted in Europe as a top contender for the post, Carlos Westendorp, Spanish ambassador to the United Nations.
Albright has said a key priority of the new U.S. initiative is greater support for the Bosnia war crimes tribunal, which she plans to visit in The Hague on Wednesday.
U.S. officials are still discussing possible creation of a special military unit to track down war criminals and this could come up in her discussions this week.
Albright is due to visit the Balkans at the weekend, including Sarajevo, Banja Luka and Brcko in Bosnia and also possibly Zagreb and Belgrade.
Her talks with de Charette and Primakov will also cover other topics, including NATO expansion and Sunday's election in Iran.
